key_insight: AI can use snoring sound features alone to distinguish palatal from epiglottic upper-airway obstruction in obstructive sleep apnea.
clinical_relevance: This suggests a non-invasive acoustic screening approach could help phenotype obstruction site when drug-induced sleep endoscopy is unavailable or impractical.
method: Retrospective analysis of 159 DISE recordings from adults with moderate, non-positional OSA
Snoring events were manually labeled by two blinded experts; only fully agreed events were kept
Spectral, cepstral, temporal, and harmonic features were selected and classified with SVM and MLP using patient-independent nested cross-validation
evidence_signal: Using 1,759 labeled snoring events (1,054 palatal; 705 epiglottic), both models reached ROC AUC 0.90 ± 0.03, with balanced accuracy of 0.83 (SVM) and 0.81 (MLP).
watch_item: The dataset came from a retrospective, highly selected DISE cohort, so real-world performance and generalizability need prospective external validation.
paper_title: The sound of snoring: AI-based acoustic phenotyping of upper airway obstruction in Obstructive Sleep Apnea
